Assessment incorporating Beige Book and SLOOS insights

- Policy stance: The FOMC kept the federal funds rate at 0–0.25% and continued Treasury ($80B/month) and agency MBS ($40B/month) purchases, aiming to achieve maximum employment and inflation moderately above 2% for some time. Policy remains data- and virus-dependent.

- Beige Book cross-district signals: Progress on vaccinations is supporting activity. Districts reported improving consumer spending and some revival in travel and tourism from low levels, with auto sales steady to higher but constrained by supply chain issues. Employment increased modestly, though labor demand varies by industry and skill, and shortages of qualified workers are acute. COVID-related supply chain disruptions and labor supply constraints remain notable headwinds, contributing to cost pressures.

- Credit conditions (SLOOS overlay): Large banks eased standards on key mortgage categories, and foreign banks reported stronger C&I loan demand—evidence of improving credit intermediation alongside accommodative monetary policy. However, banks still cite caution around the outlook and sector-specific risks, limiting the breadth of easing, especially for smaller firms and still-stressed sectors.

Bottom line: Beige Book’s modest, vaccine-assisted improvement in spending, employment, and services activity, combined with SLOOS-reported easing in mortgage credit and some demand recovery, point to a slightly stronger near-term outlook than an FSR-only read. Persistent supply chain and labor constraints and uneven sectoral recovery continue to warrant an accommodative stance.
